title: Diversity Of Life And Plant Function

sections.title: Classification and evolutionary relationships
sections.text:
Classification organizes diversity and makes comparisons possible. Traditional ranks include domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. A scientific species name combines genus and specific epithet, conventionally italicized, as in *Homo sapiens*. Classification systems change when new evidence reveals evolutionary relationships; one historical kingdom scheme should not be mistaken for an unchanging law of nature.

The three-domain framework distinguishes Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotic but differ in important molecular features. Eukarya includes animals, plants, fungi and diverse lineages often grouped informally as protists. Viruses are studied separately from cellular domains because they depend on host cells for reproduction.

Species concepts vary. The ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring is useful for many sexually reproducing organisms, but does not readily classify asexual microbes or extinct forms. Modern systematics combines morphology, molecular sequences, development and other evidence. A branching evolutionary tree represents common ancestry, not a ladder from “inferior” to “superior” organisms.

sections.title: Plant diversity and reproduction
sections.text:
Land plants share features related to life on land, including protected embryos. Nonvascular plants lack the extensive water-conducting tissues of vascular plants. Seedless vascular plants, including ferns, have transport tissues but reproduce through spores. Gymnosperms produce seeds without enclosing them in an ovary-derived fruit; angiosperms are flowering plants whose seeds develop within fruits.

| Group | Major distinguishing feature | Familiar example |
|---|---|---|
| Nonvascular plants | Lack true vascular transport system | Mosses |
| Seedless vascular plants | Vascular tissues; spores rather than seeds | Ferns |
| Gymnosperms | Seeds not enclosed in a fruit | Pines |
| Angiosperms | Flowers and fruit-enclosed seeds | Wheat, mango and roses |

Flowers contain reproductive structures. Pollen delivers the male gametophyte; pollination transfers pollen to the appropriate receptive structure. Fertilization joins gametes and differs from pollination. In flowering plants, double fertilization produces an embryo and associated nutritive tissue. Seeds protect the developing embryo and often provide reserves, while fruits assist protection and dispersal.

Plants respond to environmental signals. Shoots often grow toward light through differential growth, and roots respond to gravity and water conditions. Hormones coordinate growth, dormancy, ripening and stress responses. These responses are chemically regulated even though plants lack animal nervous systems.

sections.title: Water, minerals and sugar transport
sections.text:
Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil through interacting passive and active processes. Root hairs increase contact area. Water enters according to water-potential gradients and moves through tissues into xylem. Dissolved mineral transport depends on selective membrane proteins and electrochemical gradients, so roots do not absorb every soil chemical equally.

Xylem transports water and minerals and provides structural support. Evaporation from leaf surfaces during transpiration creates tension transmitted through cohesive water columns. Adhesion to walls and other forces help sustain the pathway. This cohesion–tension mechanism explains much long-distance ascent of water; it is not adequately explained by capillary rise alone in a tall tree.

Stomata are pores controlled by guard cells. Opening allows carbon dioxide entry for photosynthesis but also permits water loss. Closing conserves water while limiting carbon supply. Plant water use therefore involves a trade-off between gas exchange and dehydration risk. Temperature, humidity, light, wind and soil moisture influence the outcome.

Phloem moves sugars and other compounds between sources and sinks. A source exports assimilates, such as a mature photosynthetic leaf; a sink imports them, such as a growing root or developing seed. Sugar loading promotes osmotic water entry and pressure differences that drive bulk flow. A given organ can change role during development, and phloem transport is not always downward.

sections.title: Animal diversity
sections.text:
Animals are multicellular heterotrophs that obtain organic food and typically develop specialized tissues. Body symmetry, tissue organization, digestive systems, support structures and embryonic development help compare major groups. Invertebrate is a useful collective term for animals without vertebral columns, rather than one single evolutionary branch.

Sponges filter water and lack the typical true tissues of many other animals. Cnidarians, including jellyfish and corals, have specialized stinging cells and radial organization. Flatworms, roundworms and segmented worms differ in body plan. Molluscs include snails, bivalves and cephalopods. Arthropods have jointed appendages and an exoskeleton and include insects, crustaceans and arachnids. Echinoderms include sea stars and sea urchins and are related to chordates within a broader evolutionary grouping.

Vertebrates include fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Fishes use diverse aquatic adaptations; amphibians commonly have life cycles connected with moist environments; reptiles have features supporting reproduction on land; birds possess feathers; mammals have hair and mammary glands. These descriptions have exceptions and require evolutionary context: birds are nested within the reptile lineage in modern phylogeny.

sections.title: Fungi, microbes and ecological roles
sections.text:
Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb nutrients after extracellular digestion. Their walls commonly contain chitin. They include yeasts, moulds and mushrooms and differ fundamentally from photosynthetic plants. Some fungi decompose dead material, some form beneficial associations with roots and others cause disease.

Bacteria and archaea participate in decomposition, nutrient transformations and many symbioses. A microorganism is not automatically a pathogen. Gut microbes, nitrogen-fixing associations and fermentation organisms illustrate beneficial roles. Protist lineages include photosynthetic algae and heterotrophic organisms, including certain parasites. Ecological role, cell type and disease potential are different classification dimensions.

Biological diversity supports food webs, nutrient cycling and resilience, but ecosystems cannot be understood by counting species alone. Genetic diversity within species, interactions among species and the diversity of habitats all matter. Conservation therefore requires attention to both organisms and the conditions that maintain their populations.

**Adaptation, natural selection and resistance.** Populations contain heritable variation. When variants differ in survival or reproduction under particular conditions, their frequencies can change over generations. An adaptation is understood relative to an environment and evolutionary history, rather than as a conscious attempt by an organism to improve itself. Antibiotic and pesticide resistance illustrate selection on existing or newly arising variation; an individual bacterium does not acquire a useful mutation merely because it needs one.

**Comparative body systems.** Increasing body size and activity can favour internal transport and exchange surfaces because diffusion alone is effective only over limited distances. Gills, lungs and insect tracheal systems solve gas-exchange problems in different environments. Open and closed circulatory arrangements distribute materials differently. These differences are linked to body plan and ecology rather than a simple ranking of every animal on one scale of complexity.

**Plant reproduction and persistence.** Spores and seeds are not equivalent structures. A seed contains an embryo, protective tissue and commonly reserves, whereas a spore is typically a single reproductive cell. Alternation of generations describes alternating multicellular haploid and diploid stages in plant life cycles. Their relative prominence differs among plant groups, helping explain why mosses, ferns and seed plants reproduce differently while sharing deeper biological relationships.

questions.prompt: A fungus is distinguished from a typical green plant partly because fungi generally:

options.B: Obtain organic nutrients heterotrophically and have chitin-rich cell walls
options.D: Use atmospheric nitrogen as their only energy source

questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs with cell walls commonly containing chitin; plants generally use cellulose-rich walls and many photosynthesize.

questions.prompt: How does transpiration support upward movement of water in xylem?

options.B: It makes water molecules repel each other entirely
options.C: Evaporative water loss can generate tension transmitted through cohesive water columns

questions.explanation: Cohesion–tension theory explains much ascent of xylem sap through transpiration-driven pressure gradients and water cohesion.

questions.prompt: In the pressure-flow model of phloem transport, sugars move from sources toward sinks primarily because:

options.A: Osmotically generated pressure differences drive bulk flow within conducting tissues
options.D: All transport occurs by gravity alone

questions.explanation: Loading and unloading sugars create osmotic and pressure gradients that help drive phloem sap flow.
